title: Wedjat deepening: fraction-origin correction and preregistered paleographic fork
research_question: Is the familiar six-value dyadic sequence historically derived from physical parts of the Wedjat eye, or are the numerical signs and the eye motif separate traditions that were associated later?

historical_correction.popular_claim: The six dyadic capacity signs are pieces of the Eye of Horus and the eye itself encodes the fractions.

evidence.source: Jim Ritter, 'Horus-eye Fractions', Encyclopedia of Ancient History, 2012
evidence.finding: The term Horus-eye fractions is commonly applied to six signs for subdivisions of the heqat grain-volume measure, and the association with parts of Horus's eye was proposed in 1911.

evidence.source: Jim Ritter, 'Closing the Eye of Horus: The Rise and Fall of Horus-eye Fractions', Under One Sky
evidence.finding: Ritter argues that, in their origin at least, the signs should not be treated as fractions associated with the Eye of Horus; he instead discusses them as capacity-system submultiples and centers the historical question on sign forms.

evidence.source: Bibliography of Egyptian mathematics in The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus, vol. I
evidence.finding: The bibliography records Georg Möller's 1911 article 'Die Zeichen für die Bruchteile des Hohlmasses und das Uzatauge', the early publication associated with the eye interpretation.

historical_correction.consequence: The museum-amulet geometry experiment and the history-of-capacity-signs experiment must be treated as independent lanes. A fit in one lane cannot validate the other.

museum_morphology_lane.question: Do real museum-provenanced Wedjat objects exhibit a reproducible six-component geometric regularity compatible with a dyadic ladder?
museum_morphology_lane.reason: Even a geometric regularity in amulets would not by itself prove that ancient capacity submultiple signs were derived from those physical parts.

new_paleographic_lane.primary_question: Across independently dated Egyptian textual witnesses, do the six capacity-system submultiple sign forms show a reproducible formal genealogy toward or away from recognizable Wedjat-eye components?
new_paleographic_lane.unit_of_analysis: one dated sign occurrence in an independently catalogued textual witness
admission_sources: scholarly editions with plate or sign-form evidence
dated hieratic or hieroglyphic capacity notation witnesses
pre_measurement_freeze: exact image or scan SHA-256 when legally obtainable
nominal capacity value assigned from edition independently of visual resemblance
forbidden_selection: do not choose only signs that look eye-like
do not assign nominal value from resemblance to a Wedjat component
do not use modern Unicode D011-D016 shapes as historical ground truth
do not relabel components after seeing fit scores

tests.T1_chronological_stability: Does within-value sign morphology remain more similar across periods than between nominal values?
tests.T2_wedjat_component_similarity: Using frozen objective features, is each nominal sign significantly closer to its proposed Wedjat component than to the other five components under permutation?
tests.T3_time_direction: If an eye association arose late, similarity should increase in later witnesses rather than appear equally in the earliest admitted witnesses.
tests.T4_label_permutation_null: Permute the six proposed sign-to-eye-component assignments; the historical mapping must outperform the permutation distribution.
tests.T5_style_control: Compare against non-Wedjat signs of similar stroke complexity from the same documents to estimate generic scribal-shape similarity.

primary_admission_gate.failure_semantics: A failure is evidence against a stable eye-component derivation under the frozen test, not a reason to retune the mapping.

important_new_insight: The strongest next historical test is no longer 'does an amulet look binary?'. It is a paleographic genealogy test: whether the six actual capacity-submultiple signs, in dated textual witnesses, carry eye-component morphology earlier than or independently of the 1911 scholarly association.

relation_to_eye_in_the_sky.reason: The 1982 cover demonstrates modern reuse of Wedjat iconography in observation/surveillance themes but cannot serve as ancient evidence.

highest_admissible_claim: The exact dyadic mathematics is reproducible, but the popular historical premise that the six capacity submultiple signs were originally pieces of the Eye of Horus is contested in specialist scholarship and should not be assumed. The appropriate next historical experiment is a preregistered paleographic genealogy of the actual signs across dated textual witnesses, kept independent from the museum-amulet geometry lane.
next_gate: Build and seal the first 60-occurrence, 12-document paleographic corpus before scoring any sign-to-Wedjat similarity.
